items.title: Some infinities are larger than others
items.claim: There are infinitely many integers. There are infinitely many real numbers between 0 and 1. These two infinities are NOT the same size — there are strictly more reals between 0 and 1 than there are integers.
items.prompt: How can we prove the reals between 0 and 1 are 'more' than the natural numbers?

options.text: Reals have decimal places, integers don't

Cantor's diagonal argument: assume you can list all reals in [0,1] in a sequence; construct a new real by altering the nth digit of the nth listed real; this new number differs from every listed real, contradicting completeness of the list
Both infinities are exactly the same size

items.reveal:
Suppose you could list all the reals in [0,1] in a sequence: r1, r2, r3, ...
Write their decimal expansions:
r1 = 0.d11 d12 d13 ...
r2 = 0.d21 d22 d23 ...
r3 = 0.d31 d32 d33 ...
Now define a new number x = 0.x1 x2 x3 ..., where x_n is chosen to differ from d_nn (say, x_n = 5 if d_nn != 5, otherwise x_n = 6).

By construction, x differs from r_n in the nth decimal place, for every n. So x is in [0,1] but not in the list. The list cannot have contained all reals.

Georg Cantor's argument made set theory a precise discipline — and gave us cardinal numbers. The continuum is 'bigger' than the countable integers. Cantor's contemporaries (including Kronecker) attacked the idea bitterly; Cantor suffered from depression and died in a sanatorium in 1918.
items.why: All infinities are imagined as the same vague 'lots'. There are distinct, comparable sizes of infinity, and the proof uses no advanced machinery.

items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.

items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.
